idiom_name: Visitor interface with a single Visit(node) plus a type switch (or hand-named VisitX methods)
implementation_notes: Go has no method overloading, so the second dispatch cannot be encoded as one visit method per element type: either hand-name the methods (Accept(v MyVisitor) on each node and VisitFoo(f *Foo) on the visitor interface, which keeps compile-time coverage but does not scale past a handful of types), or collapse everything into one Visit(node Node) and recover the concrete type with a type switch - which is what the standard library does for go/ast, where Visitor.Visit(node) returns the visitor to continue with and Walk/Inspect drive the traversal. The single-method interface plus Inspect(func(Node) bool) is the practical default because it composes with closures and lets callers prune subtrees; the typed form is worth it for a small, closed set of your own types, where a missing method is a compile error rather than a forgotten case.
pitfalls: A type switch inside Visit loses static coverage: a new node type compiles fine and silently hits the default arm, which is the known weakness of go/ast's own design and the reason the typed Accept/VisitX form is still argued for.
Walk calls Visit(nil) after each node's children, so a visitor that dereferences its argument without a nil check panics.
Returning the same visitor from Visit continues the walk and returning nil prunes the subtree - easy to mix up, and a pruned subtree looks like a bug in the operation.
The visitor should usually be used through a pointer receiver; a value receiver on a struct holding state silently discards everything it accumulates.
